items.title: HF is a 'weak' acid that eats through glass
items.claim: Hydrofluoric acid has a pKa around 3.2 — classified as a WEAK acid. Yet it dissolves glass, etches silicon and is famously lethal.
items.prompt: Why is HF dangerous if it is a weak acid?

options.text: HF is actually a strong acid; the textbook is wrong
Acid strength (degree of ionisation in water) is separate from chemical reactivity — HF attacks Si-O bonds in glass and binds calcium in tissue, causing systemic toxicity unrelated to its pKa
HF reacts with skin's water to form a strong acid
HF only seems weak in dilute solution

items.reveal_title: Acid strength is not chemical reactivity
items.reveal:
HF's pKa around 3.2 means it only partially dissociates in water — strictly weaker than HCl, HBr, HI in that one chemical sense.

But HF's chemistry is dominated by fluoride. F- is a small, highly electronegative anion that forms exceptionally strong bonds to silicon (in glass) and beryllium and calcium. Glass etching: 4 HF + SiO2 to SiF4 + 2 H2O. HF poisoning: F- penetrates skin and chelates calcium and magnesium in blood and tissues, causing hypocalcaemia, cardiac arrest, deep necrosis.

A splash of 70 percent HF over 2 percent of body area can kill an adult.
items.why: Acidity (pKa) is the equilibrium constant for proton release in water. It tells you nothing about how reactive the conjugate base is or how toxic the molecule is.

items.title: A blacksmith's anvil works because of heat capacity, not strength
items.claim: A 100 kg steel anvil sits cold under a 1300°C glowing iron bar. The bar bends; the anvil doesn't even warm to the touch. The mass of the anvil sets the rate at which the bar cools — but each strike still leaves the anvil cool.
items.prompt: Why doesn't the heat 'flow' into the anvil and damage it?

options.text: Heat flow is finite over the brief contact time; the anvil's large heat capacity buffers any small heat input it does receive, keeping its temperature change tiny

items.reveal_title: Mass times specific heat = thermal inertia
items.reveal:
A 1 kg piece of red-hot iron at 1300°C contains about 580 kJ above ambient. Strike it once on a 100 kg anvil and transfer (very roughly) a few percent of that heat by contact. The anvil — 100 kg with specific heat 460 J/kg·K — warms by maybe 0.2°C.

Multiple strikes can heat parts of the anvil noticeably but it dissipates fast through the anvil's mass and into the ground via its sturdy base. Anvils last decades of professional use without damage.

The principle generalises: heat sinks on CPUs, heat reservoirs in steam plants, and the oceans' role as Earth's thermal flywheel all rely on the same mass-times-heat-capacity logic.
items.why: Heat is taught with single-substance examples. Real heat transfer is set by mass, specific heat, contact area and time — not just temperature difference.

items.title: Firing tissue paper at a battleship
items.claim: In 1909 Geiger and Marsden, working in Rutherford's Manchester lab, fired alpha particles at thin gold foil. Most passed through with small deflections. About 1 in 8000 bounced back. Rutherford said: 'It was almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you.'
items.prompt: What did the data force chemists to abandon?

options.text: Thomson's 'plum pudding' model, in which positive charge was spread out smoothly through the atom; backscatter required a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus
The idea that gold is a metal

items.reveal:
Rutherford's 1911 paper proposed the atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at its centre, with electrons orbiting at relatively huge distance. The nuclear radius must be smaller than 10 to the minus 14 m — about 100,000 times smaller than the atom.

Most of the atom is empty space. The plum pudding model died.

Bohr (working with Rutherford in Manchester) added quantised orbits in 1913 to explain hydrogen's discrete emission lines. Moseley (Manchester, 1913) used X-ray spectra to reorder elements by atomic number rather than atomic mass — and was killed at Gallipoli in 1915 aged 27.
items.why: Single 'crazy' experimental results can rewrite an entire model of the atom. The gold foil result was so unexpected Rutherford initially didn't believe it.
